title: Superlatives: The Best, The Most and -est Forms
summary: Choose superlatives to identify the highest or lowest degree within a group. Form -est, most and irregular superlatives, use the and possessives, distinguish in from of, and combine one of the ... with plurals or a superlative with the present perfect.
learningObjectives: Form regular and irregular superlatives and distinguish them from two-item comparatives.
Use the or a possessive with superlatives and use one of the + plural noun accurately.
Choose in for a place or group and of for periods of time following superlatives.
Use oldest and the family-specific eldest appropriately, and make natural superlative + present-perfect sentences.

explanation.heading: Superlatives select an extreme within a group
explanation.body: Use a superlative to identify one or more members at the highest or lowest degree within a stated or understood group. Most one-syllable adjectives use -est: small → smallest. Words ending in consonant + y often change to -iest: tidy → tidiest. Longer adjectives usually take most: most practical and most convenient. The group matters: a person might be the tallest in a class but not in a school.
explanation.example: This is the quietest corner in the entire building.

explanation.heading: Irregular forms and the comparative contrast
explanation.body: Good changes to best, bad to worst and far to furthest or farthest. A comparative such as safer than compares items; the superlative safest identifies the extreme in a group. Do not combine most with an -est word, and do not substitute better for best when ranking an entire group. Superlatives often work with in or of to identify the group.
explanation.example: We tested four solutions, and the third was the best.

explanation.heading: Articles, possessives and one of the ...
explanation.body: A superlative generally follows the, but a possessive can take its place: the youngest participant, our youngest participant. After one of the + superlative, use a plural countable noun, because the person or thing belongs to a larger group: one of the strongest candidates. A superlative does not always mean something is unique; several candidates may be tied.
explanation.example: Their youngest daughter is one of the fastest swimmers in her club.

explanation.heading: Where and when: in versus of
explanation.body: Use in after a superlative for a place, organisation or group: the busiest street in the neighbourhood, the newest member in the team. Use of for time periods: the wettest month of the year, the happiest weekend of my life. These prepositions mark the set being considered, not how the quality is measured.
explanation.example: It was the busiest afternoon of the entire semester.

explanation.heading: Oldest, eldest and life experience
explanation.body: Oldest is the regular superlative of old and works for people and things. Eldest is reserved mainly for family position: their eldest child or their oldest child. It does not normally describe a building. To talk about experiences up to now, a superlative is often followed by the present perfect, especially with ever: the kindest message I have ever received. Use past participles in this clause.
explanation.example: That was the most useful course I have ever taken.

comparisons.title: Two-item comparison versus a group extreme

left.label: Comparative
left.example: The silver phone is lighter than the blue one.
left.note: Lighter than compares the two specified phones.

right.label: Superlative
right.example: The silver phone is the lightest of the five models.
right.note: Lightest identifies an extreme among five models.

left.label: In + place/group
left.example: It is the busiest café in this district.
left.note: In identifies a location or group within which the café is ranked.

right.label: Of + time period
right.example: Saturday was the busiest day of the month.
right.note: Of connects the extreme day to a time period.

examples.sentence: The middle shelf holds the heaviest items in the storeroom.
examples.note: Heaviest changes the adjective heavy to an -iest superlative.

examples.sentence: Of the six routes, this one is the most convenient for cyclists.
examples.note: Convenient takes most, not an -est ending.

examples.sentence: Our eldest cousin organised the family reunion.
examples.note: Eldest refers to age order among family members.

examples.sentence: The guide showed us one of the oldest bridges in the county.
examples.note: One of the oldest is followed by the plural noun bridges.

examples.sentence: This is the funniest story I have ever heard from that presenter.
examples.note: The present perfect after the superlative refers to experience up to now.

commonMistakes.incorrect: This is the most shortest road to the station.
commonMistakes.correct: This is the shortest road to the station.
commonMistakes.why: A short adjective uses -est; do not add most before shortest.

commonMistakes.incorrect: She is one of the best designer in our company.
commonMistakes.correct: She is one of the best designers in our company.
commonMistakes.why: One of the + superlative must be followed by a plural countable noun.

commonMistakes.incorrect: It was the coldest morning in the winter.
commonMistakes.correct: It was the coldest morning of the winter.
commonMistakes.why: When a time period is the reference set, use of, not in.

commonMistakes.incorrect: That is the eldest church in the region.
commonMistakes.correct: That is the oldest church in the region.
commonMistakes.why: Eldest is for family members; oldest describes both people and buildings.

studyTips: When choosing between -er and -est, first count the items being compared and identify the group explicitly.
Read sentences aloud using one of the + plural noun, then switch between place groups with in and time periods with of.
Practise short superlative-plus-experience statements with have/has ever + past participle, such as the best ... I have ever seen.

exercises.prompt: Three backpacks cost 70, 50 and 85 reais. The 50-real backpack is ___.
exercises.feedback: Among three backpacks, the one costing fifty reais is the cheapest.

exercises.prompt: We visited five neighbourhoods. The central district had the largest crowds; it was ___.
exercises.feedback: The most crowded identifies the highest degree among the five areas.

exercises.prompt: We tried four recipes, and everyone preferred the last one. It was ___ recipe of the four.
exercises.feedback: Best is the irregular superlative of good, for the preferred recipe in a group.

exercises.prompt: Local historians say the stone bridge is ___ in the region.
exercises.feedback: Oldest applies to objects and buildings; eldest is reserved for family members.

exercises.prompt: We compared eight options. The team chose ___ proposal for the job. (practical; superlative)
acceptedAnswers: the most practical
exercises.feedback: A longer adjective such as practical takes most in the superlative.

exercises.prompt: Our classroom gets more sunlight than any other classroom in the school. It is ___ room in the school. (bright; superlative)
acceptedAnswers: the brightest
exercises.feedback: The short adjective bright takes -est with the for the highest degree.

exercises.prompt: Isabel has three brothers. Theo was born first. Theo is ___ brother. (old; use the family-specific superlative)
acceptedAnswers: the eldest
exercises.feedback: Eldest is a family-specific alternative to oldest before brother.

exercises.prompt: Every day on our trip was mild except Tuesday, when the temperature dropped sharply. Tuesday was ___ day of the trip. (cold; superlative)
acceptedAnswers: the coldest
exercises.feedback: Cold forms the superlative coldest to single out the minimum temperature.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: This is the most easy route through the park.
acceptedAnswers: This is the easiest route through the park.
exercises.feedback: Easy changes -y to -i and adds -est: easiest.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: This is one of the best restaurant in the district.
acceptedAnswers: This is one of the best restaurants in the district.
exercises.feedback: One of the best is followed by a plural countable noun.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: She is the best pianist of the orchestra.
acceptedAnswers: She is the best pianist in the orchestra.
exercises.feedback: Use in with an organisation or group of people such as an orchestra.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: This is the best exhibition I have ever visit.
acceptedAnswers: This is the best exhibition I have ever visited.
exercises.feedback: A superlative followed by the present perfect needs the past participle visited.

speakingExercises.prompt: There are three cars: a 2014 model, a 2018 model and a 2022 model. Start with “The 2014 model” and use “the oldest car”.
acceptedAnswers: The 2014 model is the oldest car.
speakingExercises.feedback: The oldest identifies the earliest car within the three-car group.

speakingExercises.prompt: You tested five tools. Tool B had the fewest failures. Begin with “Tool B” and describe it as the most reliable of the five tools.
acceptedAnswers: Tool B is the most reliable of the five tools.
speakingExercises.feedback: The most reliable expresses the highest degree within the five tools.

speakingExercises.prompt: This shop is among the top bookstores in the town. Begin with “This is” and say “one of the best bookstores in town”.
acceptedAnswers: This is one of the best bookstores in town.
speakingExercises.feedback: One of the best must be followed by a plural noun, bookstores.

speakingExercises.prompt: The heat peaked on Wednesday during one week. Begin with “Wednesday” and finish with “of the week”. Use hottest day.
acceptedAnswers: Wednesday was the hottest day of the week.
speakingExercises.feedback: Of introduces a time period after the superlative.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say a complete sentence about life experience, starting with “This is the best cake” and ending with “ever tasted”. Use the present perfect with I.
acceptedAnswers: This is the best cake I have ever tasted.
This is the best cake I’ve ever tasted.
speakingExercises.feedback: Have ever tasted connects the superlative with experience up to now.

speakingExercises.prompt: Three siblings are in one family. Elena was born first. Begin with “Elena” and describe her as “the eldest child in the family”.
acceptedAnswers: Elena is the eldest child in the family.
speakingExercises.feedback: Eldest is appropriate for a person’s position among siblings.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences using these facts. First: this road / shorter than / the other road. Second: this road / the shortest road / in the village. Begin each with “This road”.
acceptedAnswers: This road is shorter than the other road. This road is the shortest road in the village.
speakingExercises.feedback: Shorter compares two roads; the shortest identifies an extreme among all village roads.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask a question using exactly these words: “Which is the tallest building in our town?”
acceptedAnswers: Which is the tallest building in our town?
speakingExercises.feedback: The tallest ranks buildings within a defined area.

listeningExercises.audioText: We reviewed five logo designs and selected the third because it was the best overall.
listeningExercises.feedback: Best describes the third design as the winner among all five options.

listeningExercises.audioText: The central library has the most books of our three branches, although the western branch is newer.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which library location has the largest book collection?
listeningExercises.feedback: The most books of all three means the central branch has the largest collection.

listeningExercises.audioText: Nora bought the cheapest ticket available for the concert on Friday.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word superlative phrase heard immediately after “bought”.
acceptedAnswers: the cheapest
listeningExercises.feedback: The cheapest identifies the lowest-priced option among the available tickets.

listeningExercises.audioText: That community garden was one of the most rewarding projects I have ever worked on.
listeningExercises.prompt: How does the speaker describe the project?
choices: It was the only project they completed.
It was their least useful project.
It was among their most rewarding projects.
listeningExercises.feedback: One of the most rewarding marks it as among the top projects, not necessarily the single best.

listeningExercises.audioText: My eldest brother moved abroad last year, but my younger brothers still live nearby.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker mean about her brother?
choices: He is older than her other brothers.
He is the tallest in his class.
He is older than everyone in the town.
listeningExercises.feedback: Eldest brother identifies the oldest among the speaker’s brothers; it does not necessarily identify the oldest sibling overall.

listeningExercises.audioText: In my three years at this café, last July was the busiest month of all.
listeningExercises.prompt: When did the café experience its highest customer numbers?
choices: In August of the previous year.
listeningExercises.feedback: The busiest month of all identifies last July within the three-year period.

listeningExercises.audioText: The clock tower is the oldest building in our village, according to local records.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word superlative phrase heard immediately after “is”.
acceptedAnswers: the oldest
listeningExercises.feedback: The oldest identifies the building with the greatest age in the village.

listeningExercises.audioText: That’s the most interesting documentary I have ever watched about ocean life.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word superlative phrase heard immediately after “That’s”.
acceptedAnswers: the most interesting
listeningExercises.feedback: Most interesting is the superlative for the speaker’s experience with documentaries.
